progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b03: transmission routes; food and water as vehicles; the faecal-oral route. From p01: the epidemic curve (new cases by time of onset); one shared source gives a sharp cluster, person-to-person spread gives rising waves. From b10: environmental management (treating water, carrying sewage away) cuts the travel link for everyone and needs nobody to remember; isolation and quarantine; the incubation period; "Isolate the infected, quarantine the exposed." From b12: Anopheles bites mostly at night; bed nets cut bites. From b13: incidence (new cases in a set time per number of people), prevalence (share of a population with the disease at one time), "Incidence is the tap, prevalence is the tank", rates (divide by the population, then multiply). From Year 11: percentages. Not assumed: the word "denominator" (spoken with its meaning, "the number you divide by"), Clostridium perfringens and Vibrio cholerae (screen only; spoken as "this bacterium" and "cholera"), "people at risk" (spoken with its meaning).
progression.startsWith: An unfamiliar outbreak table, survey or epidemic curve. The video opens: Outbreak questions hand you a table or a graph and ask what's going on.
progression.stopsAfter: calculating the percentage ill in each lunch group at Camp Wollemi with each group's own denominator (16 of 28, about 57 per cent; 0 of 14) and evaluating the person-to-person claim from the epidemic curve (two sharp clusters, each 8 to 18 hours after a meal containing the same leftover chicken, nothing between, and none ill among salad-roll eaters who shared cabins), so one food source eaten twice, not person-to-person spread; calculating malaria incidence per 1,000 per year with the whole population as denominator (12, then 2) and prevalence of infection with the people tested as denominator (2.5 per cent, then 0.3 per cent), and explaining that bed nets cut bites and so new infections (the tap), which lowers prevalence too, while same-day testing and treatment shortens infections (the tank), so prevalence falls further, and leaves fewer parasites for mosquitoes to pick up; reading a cholera epidemic curve against two interventions (cases kept rising after household quarantine and fell within a week of chlorination and toilet repair; they did not stop at once, because people infected just before chlorination could still fall ill up to 5 days later) and justifying environmental management over quarantine (cholera travels in contaminated water; chlorine and toilets break that link for everyone; quarantine misses the many infected people with mild or no symptoms who still pass the bacteria).
progression.nextLesson: how disease control ideas have changed (route entry bio-m7-b14).

teaching.task: When an outbreak question gives you a table or a graph, how do you find the right denominator, calculate incidence and prevalence, and use the data to justify a control?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why each group's own denominator gives a fair comparison (2b); why two sharp clusters at a fixed delay after meals point to a food, not people (2c); why the salad-roll group's zero matters (shared cabins, so contact without the food gave no illness; 2c); why bed nets lower incidence (fewer bites, fewer new infections) and so prevalence too (less flowing into the tank; 3c); why faster treatment lowers prevalence further (shorter infections) and incidence too (fewer parasites for mosquitoes; 3c); why cases did not stop at once after chlorination (people infected just before it fell ill up to 5 days later; 4b); why the camp control is fast cooling (this bacterium multiplies in meat that cools slowly; 2c); why environmental management beats quarantine for cholera (the water route, and carriers with no symptoms; 4c).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Outbreak questions hand you a table or a graph and ask what is going on, and most of them turn on one habit: find the denominator, the people who could have caught it or who were tested, before comparing anything, and then link the change to a cause. Q1 (a school camp food poisoning outbreak) divides each lunch group's cases by the number who ate that lunch, reads two sharp clusters on the epidemic curve the night after each chicken meal, and so judges the claim against the sandwiches; Q2 (malaria in a province after bed nets and village health workers) calculates incidence with the whole population at risk and prevalence with only the people tested, then links each measure to the tap or the tank: fewer bites mean fewer new infections, and faster treatment shortens infections; Q3 (cholera after a flood) reads the weekly cases against the quarantine and chlorination arrows, finds the water and faeces route, and justifies chlorination and repaired toilets as breaking the travel link that quarantine does not. Each question ends with its spoken, crossed classic mistake (dividing by the whole camp, dividing positives by the whole province, quarantine works because it keeps infected people away), and the decision board gives the first move for each kind of question.
teaching.openingDecision: Outbreak questions hand you a table or a graph and ask what's going on. Most of them turn on one habit. Before you compare anything, find the denominator, the number you divide by. Then link the numbers to a cause, and the cause to a control. Here are three HSC-style questions. Pause and try each one, then we'll work through it together.
teaching.understandingCheck: Three, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a). Nothing answer-bearing during the holds.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, `docs/production/programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json`, p 55; practice and transfer only, first coverage stays with b10, b12 and b13): B7-IQ4-01: "investigate and analyse the wide range of interrelated factors involved in limiting local, regional and global spread of a named infectious disease". Q2 (malaria in a South East Asian province: vector bites, treatment and duration interact) and Q3 (cholera: water, sanitation and people with no symptoms). B7-IQ4-05: "interpret data relating to the incidence and prevalence of infectious disease in populations, for example:" with the listed examples "mobility of individuals and the portion that are immune or immunised (ACSBL124, ACSBL125)" and "Malaria or Dengue Fever in South East Asia". Q1 (outbreak percentages with the right denominator), Q2 (incidence and prevalence calculated, malaria in South East Asia), Q3 (an epidemic curve read against two interventions). B7-IQ4-04: "investigate and evaluate environmental management and quarantine methods used to control an epidemic or pandemic". Q3 (justify chlorination and toilet repair over household quarantine).

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in g03's layout: top-left the question card (stem, data and demands as an exam prints them, with the "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience" tag), readable through the whole question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Outbreak table", "Incidence and prevalence", "Epidemic curve"), hidden during each attempt. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used (no givens card). Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Q1's working is a coded lunch table with a `FractionBar` per group (filled share of a bar, the denominator written under the bar) and the coded epidemic curve (house bar chart, 4-hour onset blocks) with a meal timeline strip above it. Q2's working is a `DenominatorPair` (two stacked fraction lines, each with its denominator boxed and labelled "everyone at risk" or "people tested") and b13's `TankModel` (tap and tank). Q3's working is the coded `lineGraph` (weekly cases) with two dated intervention arrows and b10's link chain (leave, travel, enter). No people, hands or faces: students, health workers and villagers are words or plain coded dots only; the camp is the two food plates; the town is the water tank plate and a coded house outline. Coded elements are abstract only (tables, bars, axes, arrows, dots). Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): besides the question strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; each working tag fades when the next cue lands. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on and a large coded fraction writes with its denominator ringed; each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card writes with its table, epidemic curve or graph, and the chicken pasta tray, Anopheles and bed net, or Vibrio cholerae plates small at its corner; the walkthrough shrinks the card to a strip, lights the type badge and underlines each given in amber as it is used; the lunch table enlarges as each group's fraction writes, then the epidemic curve's two clusters ring against the meal times; the DenominatorPair builds the incidence and prevalence fractions and b13's TankModel shows the tap and the tank changing; the cholera graph's arrows light against the weekly bars and b10's link chain draws with the travel link broken; each classic mistake writes as a chip and takes a grey scribble cross; the check strip returns full size as the two-column decision board, row by row; scene crossfade with settle.
